title: Baucis and Philemon
text:
Jupiter and Mercury once came down to earth disguised as weary travelers, to see how people in the hill country of Phrygia treated strangers. They knocked at a thousand doors, and a thousand doors were bolted against them.

At last they reached a tiny cottage thatched with reeds. There lived Baucis and Philemon, an old couple who had married young, grown old together, and made their poverty bearable by accepting it. They took the strangers in at once. Baucis blew the embers into a fire. Philemon brought in a cabbage from the garden and took down a side of smoked bacon. They washed the guests' feet, set out olives, cheese, eggs and wine, and apologized for the humble meal.

Then they noticed that the wine bowl kept refilling itself. Frightened, they realized who their guests were, and tried to catch their only goose to serve it. The gods stopped them, revealed themselves, and led them up the hill. Below, the whole valley was drowned in a flood. Only their cottage remained, and it turned into a temple of marble and gold.

Jupiter asked what they wished for. After a quiet word with his wife, Philemon asked that they might be priests of the temple, and since they had lived together in harmony, that they might die in the same hour, so that neither would see the other's grave. Many years later, standing before the temple, each saw the other putting out leaves. They said farewell together, and became an oak and a linden, growing side by side.
lesson: A good marriage shows itself in ordinary generosity, shared together. The best wish may be not riches but simply to stay together to the end.
location: Phrygia (modern Turkey); written in Rome, Italy
